newsitem.title: USA: Skeleton found in ship used by explorer La Salle.
newsitem.headline: Skeleton found in ship used by explorer La Salle.

text.p: Archaeologists have found a nearly-intact human skeleton in the wreck of a ship that carried French explorer La Salle to what is now the Texas coast 310 years ago.
Texas Historical Commission spokeswoman Renee Peterson said discussions were under way to decide if the skeleton eventually would be sent back to France for burial.
"It's blowing our minds," Peterson said of the discovery.
She said the bones were found in late October during excavation of the ship from the shallow waters of Matagorda Bay about 80 miles (128 km) southwest of Houston.

The ship, La Belle, was anchored in the bay when it sank during a storm in 1686. Explorer Rene Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, had led an expedition there, thinking it was the mouth of the Mississippi River.
He was away on land exploring when the ship went down, but was killed a year later by mutinous members of his expedition party.
The wreck was found a year ago by a team of researchers in 14 feet (4 metres) of water near the small town of Palacios.

Archaeologists began excavating the site in September after a dam was built around the wreck and the bay waters pumped out. The ship and its contents are well preserved because they sank quickly into the seabed, where the sand and mud kept out the corrosive effects of oxygen.
Peterson said the excavation has produced a treasure trove of artifacts including cannons, pewter plates, muskets, glass beads, bronze items, pottery vessels containing food, and now, the skeleton.
"It's very, very rare to find a skeleton this intact and this old (in a shipwreck)," she said. There is a strong possibility that more human remains will be found in the ship.

"The French tradition was that even if they were travelling out at sea and they had someone die on the ship, they would store the body in the hull so it could be taken back to France to be buried on French soil," she said.
Peterson said the skeleton would be analysed to see if its identity could be determined.

Laurent Mellier, press officer for the French Consulate in Houston, told Reuters that official talks about the possible return of the skeleton to France were expected, but had not yet begun. "It will come," he said.
